title: Super flu vaccine ready as NHS regroups from busiest summer ever
description: Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.Super flu is not a medical t
body: Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.Their flu season peaks in July or August, and these countries have so far had a relatively mild year in terms of cases.Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious."Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said."With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever – and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."Everyone is at risk of catching flu. It does not matter how fit and healthy you are, or your age.Dr Doyle said: "Flu can really knock you for six, and for some children and pregnant women it can mean becoming seriously ill or ending up in hospital."The vaccine cannot give you flu. Instead, it helps your body know how to fight the virus.Children, from the age of two upwards, get a nasal spray version, while adults have an injection. A single dose is all that is needed to offer protection ahead of winter.High Street pharmacies are offering NHS flu vaccines, along with GPs and schools. People who do not qualify for a free jab can pay about £10 to £20 for one.School children and pregnant women can get a free NHS flu vaccine from September onwards. You can get a free one from October if you:are a child aged two or older who has not started school yetare aged 65 or overhave certain long-term health conditionslive in a care homeare the main carer for an older or disabled person, or receive a carer's allowancelive with someone who has a weakened immune systemare experiencing homelessness or staying in a homeless hostel or night shelterMore adults are also being offered another vaccine this winter to protect against RSV or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, which attacks the lungs.From this September, adults will be invited to have the vaccine when they are 65, rather than waiting until 75, if they have certain pre-existing health conditions, such as chronic lung disease.

schema.headline: Super flu vaccine ready as NHS regroups from busiest summer ever

title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
description: Prosecutors had argued during the trial that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not fire the gun that ki
body: Prosecutors had argued during the trial that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.They told the court that Davis had planned the shooting as retaliation after Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur and the rapper's crew in Las Vegas just hours earlier. For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now. Shakur's murder happened at a time of intense rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast rap scene and amid gang feuds between the Bloods and Crips, which had deep roots within hip-hop at the time. His family appeared emotional in court, his sister embracing a prosecutor after the verdict was read while others sat crying nearby. Outside, devoted fans of Shakur were crying and cheering. The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, where he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired. He had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace. Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.But his book and media interviews voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges being filed, with the court ruling his police interview could be used in the murder trial against him. In closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors to take Davis at his word and find him guilty. For years, he argued, Davis had been telling people "that he is responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder" through documentaries, his memoir, podcasts and a police interview."He's the shot caller - in every instance in every iteration he's the leader of the South Side Crips," Palal told the jury. "When you have the shot caller sitting shotgun when shots are fired, there's no doubt he's responsible."Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money. In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books. "There's no proof," he told the jury. But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict. Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand."I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter." The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.

schema.headline: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur

title: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByKate WhannelBusiness reporter and Nick TriggleHealth correspondentThe alarm wakes you with a shock, the summer holiday is
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByKate WhannelBusiness reporter and Nick TriggleHealth correspondentThe alarm wakes you with a shock, the summer holiday is over and it's time to face that inbox full of unread emails.This time last week, life was very different. You enjoyed late nights, lazy mornings balancing family fun and you time.Even if you enjoy your job, the transition from holiday to work can be hard, particularly in September as the days begin to shorten. Here are some ways of making the transition a little bit easier. Tick off small tasksIt can be tempting to launch straight into tackling the hardest task first.But careers coach Sarah Robinson says it's better to "ease back in" by starting with small, manageable tasks and "quick wins". "It's about trying to build momentum, because I think sometimes it can just feel overwhelming when you've got a massive inbox," she says.Counsellor Susan Carr agrees. She says it isn't possible in every industry but where viable "be a bit kinder with your expectations of what you need to do on that first day back in the office."That could mean spending the day going through emails rather than a full day of back-to-back meetings.Tara Humphrey, a primary care leadership consultant, advocates keeping her out-of-office on for her first day back."It's about hiding, if you can, just to give yourself that bit of headspace."She also says re-entry into work life can be made easier by a clearly-written out-of-office message, encouraging people to follow up when she is back in the office - that eases the stress of whether you have missed something important while on holiday. There is an alternative. She recalls a colleague who would simply delete all the emails he had been sent during his holiday. "He said, 'if people want me, they'll come back to me'."Stay touristy - but at homeCarr says it is also worth remembering what was enjoyable on holiday and "whether there's a way of integrating that more into your everyday life".While it may not be realistic to have a siesta every day, you could try cooking some Spanish food, she suggested. She also recommends holding on to the curiosity we have when in a new place and trying to be a tourist in our own area. "If we go away somewhere else... we might be looking at the architecture, visiting buildings, and I think - and I know I'm guilty of this in Manchester - we don't always appreciate what's on our doorstep."Psychotherapist Dr Joy Conlon, who runs wellbeing coaching service Alive 365, agrees."Bring one restorative part of the holiday home with you. This might be an evening walk, eating without looking at a screen, reading before bed instead of being on a screen or just spending more time outdoors. Reflect on your roleRather than treating the symptoms, it may be worth looking at the root cause of the back-to-work blues.Before, she was a counsellor, Carr worked as a solicitor. "I was vaguely aware before I went on holiday that things weren't right and I was quite stressed," she says."I went away on holiday and then I came back and suddenly I was in floods of tears every day. It wasn't just a case of needing time to adjust, it was a sign I needed a rethink."But how can you tell between a temporary nostalgia for long lie-ins and genuine unhappiness with your job?"It probably sounds really obvious," Carr says, "but I suppose one of the signs of that is how long it goes on for.""It's that length of time but also maybe the intensity of the feelings."Lying on a sunbed, it can be easy to fantasise about quitting everything and retraining as a scuba diver instructor or yoga teacher, but Carr warns against a "knee-jerk reaction". "It's about taking time and reflecting on how you might go about making a change."Book your next holiday – and make it activeIt is not just the holiday itself that makes them so enjoyable and beneficial, the anticipation of going also plays a key role, says Dr Mark Williamson, chief executive officer of Action for Happiness, a charity.And what type of holiday or how long you go for can make a difference to the overall impact.Williamson points to what he says is "genuinely surprising" research , externalwhich suggests physically active holidays may be better for wellbeing than simply lying by the pool."If you include some walking, cycling, swimming, exploring you're more likely to get back feeling refreshed," he adds.Another factor to consider is the length of your next break, he says. "Longer breaks give a bigger boost, but it seems to fade faster, partly because you return to a bigger mountain. "There's some evidence that shorter but more regular breaks bring more wellbeing benefits. The refresh from five days away may feel not far off ten, but you can do it twice as often."

schema.headline: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues

title: John Galliano exhibition at New York's Met cancelled after backlash
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"ByIan YoungsCulture
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterJohn Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.'I remain deeply sorry'At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it."I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture."It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday."John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said."I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."'Misguided'Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano."From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community."This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided"."Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

schema.headline: John Galliano exhibition at New York's Met cancelled after backlash

title: Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously
description: The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope
body: The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope their loved ones can be found alive.Rescuers continued battling to reach them on Monday, using explosives to blast into the hillside before pumping air into the Trishuli-3A site – fearing a critical window to reach survivors is closing."I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.It comes as the death toll from the flood disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border reached 939, according to the country's disaster management authority.The agency also revised its estimate of the number of missing to 3,925, of whom 592 are foreign nationals.Roughly one in seven missing people are believed to be workers at the hydropower plants. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved."I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur.Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said.Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier.A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but withdrew after finding no one there."The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur. "It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added.Rescue operations had been "intensified", Nepalese leader Shah said, noting that the floods were "not an ordinary" event."This incident indicates that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change."It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change," Shah wrote in a Facebook post late on Monday.Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit."Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved."Only 4% of the 900 bodies that have been found so far have been identified, a spokesperson from the Ministry of Health told BBC Nepali. In Chitwan, a district far downstream from where the floods first hit, makeshift burials were taking place after the Himalayan nation's river systems brought nearly 300 dead bodies to its banks.The air was thick with the smell of decay, as men wearing white Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including masks carried unidentified corpses into trucks.Over the weekend, a large portion of the forest outside the city was dug up. Medical staff and volunteers worked to extract DNA from the unidentified remains.Ganesh Aryaal, the chief district officer, told BBC Nepali that relatives will still be able to extricate the remains of their loved ones, once they are identified through DNA testing."We don't have enough freezers here... We had to choose this last alternative of temporary burial system. We are really overwhelmed," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously

title: Holy Cross: School dispute was 'hatred at its worst' says Priest
description: The priest who helped shield schoolgirls during the 2001 Holy Cross dispute has said the "hurt" of that ordeal could happen again.Speaking on the 25th
body: The priest who helped shield schoolgirls during the 2001 Holy Cross dispute has said the "hurt" of that ordeal could happen again.Speaking on the 25th anniversary of Holy Cross, Fr Aidan Troy said that possibility is what keeps him "devoted to dialogue, to conversation, to searching for justice and to caring about people". Fr Aidan said the sectarian dispute was "hatred at its worst". It happened in north Belfast when loyalist protesters tried to block the route taken by Holy Cross school pupils and their parents, who were from a Catholic background, on their walk to class. Following the initial violence, the police and Army put up crash barriers to keep a corridor route open for the Holy Cross pupils.The images of terrified schoolgirls having to run the gauntlet between lines of armoured police officers in order to get to their primary school were beamed around the world.Protestants claimed that Catholics were attacking their homes and said the school protest was their way of highlighting their concerns.Stones, bottles, fireworks and even a blast bomb were thrown during weeks of unrest.Fr Aidan, who was parish priest in Ardoyne at the time, told BBC News NI that "none of us want to see hatred"."Hatred is the rawest, smelliest, most awful thing that anyone stood in the middle of," he said."We tell this story, not to blame, but to say we are capable of doing this to each other but let's make a commitment that we never will and we'll not do anything that would ever demean the way those children were demeaned."He said people come up to him and thank him for what he did."I am embarrassed because I didn't do anything really worthwhile," he said."People say their children were given dignity. They were worth going in the front door and they were worth fighting for, and you stood in the middle of the road and said so."He added that "it could happen again"."The shock of Holy Cross, even 25 years later, probably means that it probably would not happen [again] in the exact same form, but the hurt is always possible," he said.

schema.headline: Holy Cross: School dispute was 'hatred at its worst' says Priest

title: The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial
description: Image source, ReutersByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsLindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five w
body: Image source, ReutersByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsLindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five weeks.The 36-year-old former nurse killed her three small children in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts.Charged with three counts of first-degree murder, she does not dispute killing her two sons and daughter in 2023.But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong.The prosecution, on the other hand, argues Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment.On Monday morning, a jury of nine women and three men will continue to deliberate, with several options before them:not guilty not guilty by reason of insanityfirst-degree murdersecond-degree murdermanslaughterNot guilty / not guilty by reason of insanityThis hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice after giving birth to her youngest child that told her to kill the children.Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind.Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility.Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong.A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital."The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said.Figure caption, Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?First-degree murderThis is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.As Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, put it to the BBC, Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if they pick this outcome.Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or cruelty or premeditation or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors.In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor.Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong.Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children.Second-degree murderThis is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law.It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning."For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said.In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole.ManslaughterThe jury received yet another option when the judge allowed them to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution.Manslaughter, which is defined as causing death by an unintentional, mistaken or neglectful act, carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said."This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said.The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

schema.headline: The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial

title: The Millennials swapping doom-scrolling for gardening
description: Image caption, Hannah says gardening helped her to navigate griefByMegan DaviesBBC News Updated 31 August 2026When Hannah Matthews lost her father and
body: Image caption, Hannah says gardening helped her to navigate griefByMegan DaviesBBC News Updated 31 August 2026When Hannah Matthews lost her father and grandmother in the space of a year, she found comfort in her back garden."My mind would be really busy, and I'd suddenly be out here at 7am pulling up weeds," said the 31-year-old.She is now an enthusiastic gardener, and one of thousands of young people sharing their green-fingered ways on social media. Hannah, who has more than 70,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok, said the gardening community was "booming" and represented a way of "recapturing some space that feels less tense" on social media platforms. "It brings me joy, and hopefully when someone else is just kind of doom-scrolling, they get a bit of serenity in their day as well," she said.Image caption, Hannah says the gardening community is "booming""I was born in '95, so my generation are the kind of ones who know what it's like to grow up with both analogue life and digital culture," said Hannah, from Newport.She said hobbies such as cooking, sewing and gardening were her generation's "rejection of this hyper-digital world that feels really all-consuming". She said it was a "tough time for young people" due to the cost of living, climate change, a "dire" jobs market and AI."I'm not saying we've had it harder than all other generations," she said."But it is challenging being young and maybe having different expectations to those that our parents and grandparents' generations had, and different opportunities."Hannah said gardening offered a "safe space" to "take control of your little space of land or your balcony or your pots in the kitchen or whatever you're able to have". It became that for her, she said, when she experienced the loss of her father and grandmother in 2023. "I didn't use gardening as a conscious means of therapy but I kind of just found myself out here, pottering around," she said."It's cliché but kind of creating and nourishing new life and new growth is just really the circle of life."Image source, Hannah MatthewsImage caption, Hannah says gardening can be done "in whatever space you have"Hannah considers gardening to be similar to preparing for a race."You'd normally train for a marathon 16 weeks out, which is roughly a season ahead, which is kind of how gardening works as well. "You're planning joy into your life for the next season to be bountiful." She acknowledged that owning a house and having access to outdoor space was "a real privilege". "When I first starting posting I had some comments 'It must be nice, bank of mum and dad' sort of thing."I hope to inspire that gardening can kind of be done in whatever space you have - pots on the kitchen window sill, things like that - just the act of making something with your hands and planning it and seeing it flourish is amazing." Image source, Naomi SaundersImage caption, Naomi's love of gardening has taken her to events such as the RHS Chelsea Flower ShowNaomi Saunders from Felinheli, Gwynedd, started gardening during lockdown and quickly found herself in possession of more than 300 houseplants."I started documenting my houseplants and my veg on Instagram quite early and gardening definitely was not a massive thing then," said Naomi, 32.She has since gained thousands of followers, and was recently invited to the RHS Chelsea Flower Show to create content. She thinks young people in particular are drawn to gardening content because they're "more conscious now of putting their phones down". "It's an online community that really supports each other as well," she added. "Gardening is something where people genuinely want each other to do well." Image source, Rachel GriffithsImage caption, Gardening has helped Rachel through challenges over the last few yearsFor Rachel Griffiths, 37, gardening became a "crutch" in 2020 when the "world was very crazy" due to the pandemic. The mum-of-two from Church Village, Rhondda Cynon Taf, said she had navigated postnatal depression, anxiety and undiagnosed neurodivergence over the last few years, but gardening had offered her hope. "I didn't need to make plans with friends, didn't need to try and see people, didn't have to get dressed, have a shower, and make a big deal about going out."She said when the baby was asleep, she could "pop into the garden for 5 minutes" and have a "little moment" to herself. She said the garden had also given her family hope during this summer's extreme heat."I'm not going to save the world with my garden but maybe if everybody had a little go, then it would help," she said."There are so many little things you can do at home which do make a difference." Image source, Georgia FeatherstoneImage caption, The Girlie Gardening Club recently met up at RHS Wisley in SurreyWhen Georgia Featherstone, 26, moved to a new area for work, she was initially unsure of how to make new friends and decided to start a gardening club for women. "The current gardening clubs that are out there are for people with a lot more horticultural experience, more experts, and a lot older," said Georgia.In the last two months, more than 450 people have since joined her Girlie Gardening Club group chat in order to attend local events in Surrey. "If you're a millennial, or you're the older part of Gen Z, you're kind of over going out to the pub every weekend," she said.Georgia is hoping to plan more events in the future, including talks from horticulturalists and floristry lessons. "With social media, everyone feels connected, but also so disconnected at the same time."You can swap knowledge, you can share seeds and cuttings, and that's when you really get the best of the hobby."People are looking for community and gardening brings that."

schema.headline: The Millennials swapping doom-scrolling for gardening

title: Lowestoft rollercoaster beaks down with 27 people being rescued
description: Park visitor Richard Lines said he was on another ride close to Wipeout, when a power cut appeared to affect multiple rides.Lines said he saw a worker
body: Park visitor Richard Lines said he was on another ride close to Wipeout, when a power cut appeared to affect multiple rides.Lines said he saw a worker subsequently tending to the ride, which was stationary, and this moment can be seen in video footage shared with the BBC.The carriages then begin moving again, but within seconds, they can be seen slowly rolling back and forth, before coming to a standstill.Lines said the fire service used an aerial ladder to free the passengers one-by-one."You feel sorry for the ones that were either at the front or the back who were up there for a good three hours - which is a long time," said Lines, from Wymondham in Norfolk, who was visiting with his two children.The fire service said by 17:10 they had rescued all 27 passengers and that no-one was injured.

schema.headline: Lowestoft rollercoaster beaks down with 27 people being rescued

title: Grand Canyon flash flood kills two and sparks search for missing hikers
description: Two people have died and 14 remain missing or unaccounted for after flash flooding swept through parts of the Grand Canyon, the National Park Service
body: Two people have died and 14 remain missing or unaccounted for after flash flooding swept through parts of the Grand Canyon, the National Park Service (NPS) has said.The flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon, wiping out footbridges and propelling boulders downstream.The body of a 46-year-old man was found on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said. Sixty-two people have so far been airlifted out of the area."The whole thing was terrifying," said Nikki Baggs, 41, who was among those to be airlifted out of the bottom of the Grand Canyon with her two friends. "It was a beautiful day and then people were screaming, running," she told the BBC.Baggs said she and her friends had just dropped off their belongings at a cabin in Phantom Ranch - a remote lodge at the bottom of the Grand Canyon - when they decided to venture out to enjoy the nice day. Before they knew it, a flood of water was sweeping through the area. As soon as the rain hit, Baggs and her friends headed toward higher ground, where they sat at a picnic table, before rangers yelled to them to run again to a different ledge, where they waited with others for hours before they were evacuated at around 21:30 local time (04:30 GMT).Baggs said she and her two friends had been looking forward to a steak dinner at Phantom Ranch - but were now just grateful to be alive thanks to a swift response from park rangers. "It was a really uniquely co-ordinated effort," she said. "That's what made us feel safe about all of it in an unsafe situation." Baggs said she and her friends watched from higher ground as bridges were swept away. In a statement on Monday, the NPS said search and rescue efforts continue. The recent rains in the Grand Canyon area, and more widely in south-western parts of the US, are due to monsoonal showers.A change in wind direction at this time of year pulls warm, moist air northward from the Gulf of California and the tropical Pacific, triggering storms over mountainous terrain. The storms are difficult to pinpoint in forecasts and so can strike without warning. But because the ground is usually very dry, any heavy downpours lead to dangerous flash flooding and frequent lightning which increases the threat of wildfires.Flood watches from the National Weather Service cover large parts of Arizona, as well as New Mexico, Utah and Colorado. There are lots of showers currently showing on the weather radar and these downpours will continue during Monday.The threat of flooding is something that will remain for many more weeks. The North American monsoon season usually runs to the end of September.Joey Martin told the BBC that he was at the Grand Canyon working on a transcanyon pipeline project when dense, grey clouds rolled in.He described rain "coming down so hard and so thick that you couldn't see the Grand Canyon walls".  "You couldn't see anything," Martin said. Visibility returned roughly 30 minutes later, he said. That's when he saw the creek begin to rise. It eventually turned into a torrent of mud and debris that slammed into a nearby bridge connecting Martin's work site to his living quarters."From where we were standing, it looked to be about 15ft tall," he said. "That wall of debris ended up taking out the bridge right there." Martin said he and roughly 16 other workers were there and coordinated with NPS once it became clear conditions were unsafe. They gathered hikers in the area and headed for higher ground.Eventually all were airlifted out. "It was scary," he recalled. "Never been in any kind of vicinity of something like that to that caliber," he said. "Staying calm was hard, but everybody kind of played a part in keeping people calm and keeping people, you know, focused on just getting away from the danger."The NPS initially said it was looking for information about 15 people who were thought to be missing or unaccounted for. It reported that flooding had caused significant damage in some areas and that trails in the area have been closed. Overnight guest lodgings in the South Rim will be stopped from Monday until further notice as the floods have caused "extensive damage" to the national park's water infrastructure. On Monday, the NPS said that preliminary assessments indicate about 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, which delivers water for visitors and approximately 2,500 residents, was damaged or destroyed in the flood. The NPS asked anyone who knew of hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on Saturday to get in touch.

schema.headline: Grand Canyon flash flood kills two and sparks search for missing hikers

title: England v Pakistan: Tourists drop seven players, call up seven and release coach Sarfaraz Ahmed
description: Pakistan have responded to their series defeat by England by taking the extraordinary step of dropping seven players, calling up five uncapped players
body: Pakistan have responded to their series defeat by England by taking the extraordinary step of dropping seven players, calling up five uncapped players and releasing their head coach.After two one-sided defeats in the first two Tests, the tourists have revamped their squad and backroom staff for the third and final match of the series at Edgbaston.Five of the players dropped - Muhammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman and Khurram Shahzad - have featured in the series so far, while Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Jafar have been sent home without playing.A total of seven players have been called up. Batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have previous Test experience and join the quintet of uncapped newcomers.Spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas, left-arm seamer Mohammed Imran Jr, wicketkeeper Said Baig and all-rounders Mohammad Imran and Razaullah have all received call-ups.In addition, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul have been released to be replaced by Pakistan white-ball coach Mike Hesson and former Australia seamer Ashley Noffke.The third Test in Birmingham begins on 9 September.Pakistan have been abject in the opening two Tests, losing the first at Headingley by an innings and the second at Lord's by 194 runs. They have been bowled out for less than 200 in each of their four innings.The response is remarkable. For a touring team to send home seven players and the head coach mid-series is unprecedented.Ex-Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja, also a former chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm trying to convince myself this is all OK, but it is not. "It just shows Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button. It's not good for the game, it's not good for the confidence of the players who have come in, or the for the players who are left, because it makes you a selfish team."What is the guarantee they will get the results? Some of these guys have not played Test cricket. I've got no idea why this was done."Pakistan have a history of making eccentric decisions in the wake of defeats. On England's last tour of Pakistan in 2024, the hosts responded to losing the first Test, when England made a total in excess of 800, by playing the second Test on the same pitch in Multan.On that occasion, Pakistan used garden heaters and fans to dry the surface, to assist their spinners. The home side won the next two Tests to win the series 2-1.Now, among the seven players sent home are Salman, who captained in the first Test in the absence of the injured Babar Azam, then was dropped for the second.Also dropped is opener Imam-ul-Haq, who was criticised at Lord's for not attempting to bat in either innings after suffering a calf injury while fielding on the opening day.Raja, who played 57 Tests between 1984 and 1997, added: "I'm really not happy with the situation."How many times have we seen this happen in world cricket? Never, ever. This is more like football, midway through the season, firing a manager."If you ask me how things can be fixed, I've got no idea."The sweeping selection changes come after the Pakistan team were surrounded by controversy during the second Test.At lunch on the first day, the PCB threatened to cancel the remainder of the match and tour because of an interview with the sons of Imran Khan that was broadcast by Sky.Imran, the former Pakistan captain and prime minster, has been in prison for three years on charges of corruption, which he denies.Pakistan ultimately completed the Test, with both captain Babar and head coach Sarfaraz denying any knowledge of a planned boycott.The tourists are also due to have an audience with King Charles at Clarence House this week.

schema.headline: England v Pakistan: Tourists drop seven players, call up seven and release coach Sarfaraz Ahmed

title: Heaton Park synagogue attack memorial service attended by 800
description: Hundreds remember synagogue attack victimsImage source, Family handoutsImage caption, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, were killed in the attack on t
body: Hundreds remember synagogue attack victimsImage source, Family handoutsImage caption, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, were killed in the attack on the Heaton Park Synagogue in ManchesterByJudith MoritzSpecial correspondentDaniel WittenbergSenior producer and Angela FergusonNorth WestThe Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner were among about 800 people who attended a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.Relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors were among the speakers at Monday's service of remembrance at the synagogue in Manchester.Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation – and British Jews more widely – feeling increasingly vulnerable.Two seats remained empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, In a service packed bar the two empty seats for those killed, the bereaved spoke of their lossSherelle Dresner, representing the family of Melvin Cravitz, spoke of the "lonely" and "overwhelming" new world she and her family faced in the aftermath of the attack."I have heard this new existence be described by survivors and bereaved families of other terrorist attacks as a club that no-one wants to be a part of; a club that no-one would ever choose to belong to," she said.She said she had received antisemitic abuse and "these messages should worry us all, that there are people out there justifying his murder and blaming this on his religion".Dresner praised those who "put your own lives at risk" on the day to save others, including a woman who ran "towards danger" to help Melvin.The chief rabbi, in his address to the service, said: "The attacker came here feeling positive, comfortable in his ways, encouraged and inspired by a tone of deep antisemitism within our society."We know so well how hateful thoughts can be translated into hate speech which, in turn, is only one step away from hate crime."Image source, EPAImage caption, Rabbi Daniel Walker welcomed King Charles to Heaton Park on 20 October 2025In a message read out at the start of the service, King Charles said: "My wife and I hold all those whose lives were so tragically disrupted by that terrible day most closely in our thoughts and prayers."Though the months have passed, the sense of shock and sorrow remains undiminished."The memory of those who lost their lives, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, and of those who were injured, Andrew Franks, Bernard Agyemang and Yoni Finlay, remain especially vivid in my mind."He concluded: "Hatred can never prevail over our shared humanity."Raphi Bloom, chair of the Yom Kippur Commemoration, said the service was "not only about remembrance" but was also about resilience and "honouring Melvin and Adrian by ensuring that Jewish life continues to flourish".He said "the wounds remain, but so does our spirit" and, together, they were sending a simple message that they would not be intimidated, defined by hatred or "driven from the place we have called home for more than two centuries"."As Jews we will stand tall, united, proud and strong," he said.Image caption, Raphi Bloom was among the speakers addressing hundreds of people at Heaton Park synagogue Angela Rayner referenced other "sickening terrorist attacks" across the world when she told the congregation: "These acts are a crisis for us all - they reflect the increase we've seen in obsessive, intense hatred of Jews."She said "any attack on Jews is an attack on all of us"."Together we can overcome and defeat antisemitism – and we will never rest, until every Jewish person is safe."She said this was "a hatred we must stand robustly against, and root out from its very foundations", which meant "taking on extremists and bearing down on those who seek to divide our communities"."The only way we can root out this poison is through a whole of society approach."Image caption, Yoni Finlay said Jewish people are "having to hide their identity"Yoni Finlay, who was hit by a stray police bullet while helping to barricade the doors during the attack, said: "An evil person tried to destroy us on Yom Kippur and together we have not let that evil win."When I was lying on the floor in the foyer, just through those doors, with four of my organs badly damaged by a bullet that had gone through me, I made myself a promise, that I would not die, this is not where my life was going to end."But I could not do this on my own, and neither could the shul. We could only do this with the support of the people around us."He said he was lucky enough to have an amazing family, "but we are also an incredible community"."I realised that maybe, just maybe, we were going to be okay, when we showed that rather than being stopped, we were more together than ever".Earlier, asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about how the Jewish community in the UK feels almost a year on, he said: "I don't think things feel safer, I think we certainly live behind ever increasing gates, more security than we've ever had."Jewish people are having to hide their identity. Even my own son, who's in college at the moment, has faced death threats."Image caption, The service took place ahead of the religious anniversary, rather than following the secular calendarOther speakers at the memorial service included Alan Levy, who helped barricade the doors against the attacker, and Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson.Although the first anniversary of the Heaton Park attack is not until October, the Jewish community will mark it on the religious anniversary rather than by the secular calendar.The attack happened on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, which falls in September this year.Rabbi Walker said the service was being held because the community also wanted to hold a public memorial before the Jewish High Holy Days, both to ensure those affected are remembered by wider society and to call for change in society.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

schema.headline: Heaton Park synagogue attack memorial service attended by 800

title: Mikel Arteta: Arsenal boss joins elite list of managers, but where does he rank?
description: When thinking of the greatest managers of the Premier League era, Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola are names that belong high on the
body: When thinking of the greatest managers of the Premier League era, Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola are names that belong high on the list.They are three of the rare breed to have managed 250 games with a single Premier League club, and Mikel Arteta is now the 10th member of that elite group.Monday's 1-0 win over Aston Villa was the 250th top-flight game in charge for Arteta with the Gunners, and his champions delivered a trademark performance.At full-time at Villa Park, the travelling supporters sang about how they are going to win the league again with Arteta in charge.With Arsenal coming into this season as trophy holders, and with transition affecting rivals Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea and Manchester United, it is hard to see how the fans' partisan prediction is going to be proved wrong.Arsenal conceded the fewest goals in the league last season as they won the title for the first time in 22 years.And during Arteta's nearly seven years in charge, the Gunners have become renowned for their defensive excellence.Against Aston Villa they showed it again, without allowing a shot on target against them as Bukayo Saka's second-half goal secured victory.The latest win not only puts Arteta in the 250 club. He also has the fourth-best win percentage among those bosses, with only Guardiola, Ferguson and Jurgen Klopp ahead of him.Arteta is the longest-serving current Premier League manager and with his longevity has come an Arsenal identity.Arsenal have become renowned for being difficult to break down and new players repeatedly say that they are impressed and sometimes overwhelmed by the level of detail coming from Arteta.This is the fifth season in a row where Arsenal have won their first two Premier League matches and they again have a solid platform to build another title challenge.The Gunners have only faced three shots on target in their first two Premier League games. Villa drew a blank in that regard.During their title triumph last season, the Gunners did not allow their opponents a shot on target in six league matches, the joint-most of any side in a campaign on record since the 2003-04 season.Goalkeeper David Raya has won the the Golden Glove award for the most clean sheets in each of the past three seasons, while William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes have been voted in the PFA team of the year for the past three seasons too.Since the start of March, the Gunners have kept eight Premier League clean sheets – three more than any other side and the only side in Europe's big-five leagues to have kept more are Juventus with nine."It's how they defend as a team and how they attack as a team," Arsenal's record goalscorer Thierry Henry told Sky Sports after the game."One thing is sure with Arsenal - everybody needs to run. You don't have any passengers in that team. This is how you win a title. You can see they are so good at it."Arsenal have one of the best squads in Europe. The Gunners spent £250m last summer bringing in eight players as they won the title and have already spent about £200m this year, turning Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m), signing Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United (£75m), Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge (£34m) and bringing in Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m)."That is what we need," Arteta said, speaking to Sky Sports when asked about his squad depth."The players that come in make the difference. All of them contributed to create more dominance and more momentum."The level of focus and the way they want to contribute to the team, that is going to be decisive in the season."Arsenal's strength in depth cannot be understated, but one area they may still look to strengthen in is the forward area.The Gunners have been on the hunt for an elite forward to lift their attack and still could be active on Tuesday's deadline day.They had an unsuccessful pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr, while they also have a long-standing interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez."We are trying to improve the squad and until tomorrow night we will try to do it," Arteta said."I have been disconnected from the world for the last 24 hours because my energy has to be on the match, but I will get back on it now."When pushed about a deal for Alvarez, Arteta said: "I don't know, that's for the people upstairs."Whatever happens in Arsenal's search, they are going to be hard to keep off the top of the table with Arteta at the helm.

schema.headline: Mikel Arteta: Arsenal boss joins elite list of managers, but where does he rank?

title: More cells being built within prisons to help tackle overcrowding
description: The government is spending £110m on creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding. The mone
body: The government is spending £110m on creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding. The money, which has been "fast-tracked from existing budgets", will be used to speed up the construction of hundreds of new prison places, the Ministry of Justice has said.Existing space within prisons, such as unused office space, laundry rooms and storage areas, will be converted into cells.The announcement comes at a time of crisis for the prison system, which is close to maximum capacity, with the government being criticised for its handling of an early release scheme. Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government would be "getting spades in the ground quicker to deliver thousands more places to lock up dangerous criminals and keep the public safe".Norris said: "This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we've already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years."We're now investing to boost these efforts further."Investment to create more prison spaces was announced as part of the government's 2025 spending review, which covered plans for the period from 2024‑25 to 2029‑30. As part of this, it allocated a £7bn capital investment to create 14,000 prison places by 2031. The £110m announced on Monday is not a new investment, and is being drawn from money previously announced. The Lord Chancellor will update Parliament on Tuesday, setting out changes to upcoming sentencing reforms which will block hundreds more dangerous offenders from earlier release.Measures also include plans to remove foreign national offenders more quickly, and ending the historic injustice of Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences in a way that balances fairness and public safety, the government has said.Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "It is absurd for Labour to talk about a 'prison building boom' when there are 700 fewer prison places than a year ago."In a matter of weeks thousands of dangerous criminals will be released onto our streets thanks to Andy Burnham, including perpetrators of some of the most vile crimes."An extra £18.9m investment into vital services for victims will also be announced to Parliament. The services will provide the specialist emotional and practical support needed to help victims move on with their lives, according to the Ministry of Justice (MoJ). This money will be reprioritised from existing budgets and will be on top of the £550m already announced by government for this support. The MoJ also announced that it had signed a contract to start building a new jail for 1,700 hundred inmates in Lancashire.On Monday, the Conservatives warned that dangerous criminals could be freed under the government's early release scheme, which aims to reduce overcrowding in prisons in England and Wales. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the weekend that anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the early prisoner release scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.Burnham said prison space would be found by releasing some inmates serving IPPs as well as by deporting foreign prisoners.Some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being released in tranches from October.The numbers due to be released has been reduced after the government said rapists, those found guilty of serious child sex offences and grooming offences and now those found guilty of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme.Timothy told the BBC that to prevent one group of dangerous criminals being released early, Burnham was "looking at releasing a different group of dangerous prisoners".Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will do nothing that would risk the public or put the public at danger."

schema.headline: More cells being built within prisons to help tackle overcrowding

title: Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterVictoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time s
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterVictoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time since she founded it in 2008, the company has said.Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd, which is led by the former Spice Girl as creative director, made an operating profit of £7.3m in 2025, accounts show, after years of losses."We have all worked hard for a long time for this moment of profitability and growth," Lady Beckham told the Financial Times, external."We've been very transparent about the problems that we had in the business but have recovered and are now growing at a sensible pace. After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand any more."Skincare successLast year, a Netflix documentary told the story of her attempting to establish a fashion brand and achieve profitability - and the series itself helped boost sales, "with particularly strong momentum in denim and jersey", according to the accounts.The fashion side of the company delivered "strong double-digit growth" overall in 2025, they said, while the beauty side, which launched in 2019, "delivered one of its strongest performances to date".That was led by the popularity of her Foundation Drops, which had a 25,000-strong waiting list and which doubled the size of the skincare part of the company.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Victoria Beckham on the catwalk at one of her brand's fashion shows in Paris in 2023The Netflix documentary showed the former pop star talking about her attempts to overcome doubters to be taken seriously as a designer and entrepreneur, then running into financial trouble when the company was "tens of millions in the red".The business was bailed out by her husband Sir David, who told the programme: "For her to have to come to me and say, 'Can I have some... We need some more money, the business needs more money' - that was hard for both of us because I didn't have the money to keep doing this."Lady Beckham said: "If he hadn't believed in me I wouldn't still have a business now."She went on to get £30m investment by selling 30% of the company to NEO Investment Partners in 2017, who launched a restructure.'Significant milestone'That included tackling what Beckham admitted was "mindblowing" waste, including "flying chairs from one side of the world to another" and spending what NEO's David Belhassen said was "70,000 a year" on office plants.In a statement on Monday, Belhassen, who is chairman of Victoria Beckham Holdings, said: "With two complementary growth engines in fashion and beauty, an increasingly international customer base and a focused operating model, the business is powerfully positioned for its next phase of profitable growth."CEO Sybille Darricarrère Lunel said: "Achieving our first operating profit is a landmark moment for Victoria Beckham and reflects several years of disciplined execution and strategic investment."Delivering this result against a more challenging luxury market and macro backdrop makes it an even more significant milestone for the business."

schema.headline: Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years
